tier_reason: BENCH.md on the c-stl-comparison result branch has STL rows (std::unordered_map, std::vector, std::set, std::string via g++/libstdc++) next to M*LIB rows, with public harness code (bench/bench-mlib.c, bench/bench-stl.cpp, bench/common.c, bench/Makefile with -O2 -march=native, best of 3), the CPU model (AMD EPYC 7763, lscpu line) and a GCC toolchain (cc/c++ on the ubuntu-latest GitHub Actions image per .github/workflows/ci.yml). Every number in claimed_speedup matches the page; the only gap is that the GCC version is printed only in the CI log (sign-in needed), not on the page.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: bench/Makefile: CFLAGS=-O2 -march=native -Wall; C side built with `cc -std=c11`, STL side with `c++ -std=c++11` (g++ and libstdc++ on the GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest image per .github/workflows/ci.yml, which runs `cc -v` but shows the output only in the CI log, viewable after sign-in); each bench run with --quiet --best --repeat 3. The GCC version is not in BENCH.md. The 'Compiler used is GCC 16.1' line in the c-stl-comparison README belongs to its code-size comparison, not to the CI benchmark run (the wiki link Benchmark-result showed the README content with no compiler version for the benchmark). The M*LIB README graphs state GNU C++ STL v10.2.
corrections.hardware: AMD EPYC 7763 64-Core Processor (lscpu line in BENCH.md; GitHub Actions ubuntu-latest runner per ci.yml; the latest result commit 7012595 was published by the CI run of 2026-08-10); an i5-3210M result is also published in the repo (master branch bench/doc/BENCH.md).
corrections.caveats: Benchmark harness is the library author's own repo (P-p-H-d/c-stl-comparison), run on a shared GitHub-hosted CI VM (run of 2026-08-10), so timings are noisy and no CPU pinning is stated; the GCC version is printed only in the CI log, not in BENCH.md (the README's 'GCC 16.1' refers to the code-size comparison). STL rows use default std::hash (identity for integers), no reserve() and operator[] inserts, so the 12.6x U64 gap is partly default-std::unordered_map node-allocation cost, and other open-addressing C++ maps would narrow it (Boost unordered flat map is 1464.12 ms on the same page, 7.97x faster than STL; KLIB khash 1257.84 ms). The 'dict Bulk' row uses M*LIB's bulk API, not the plain per-key loop. M*LIB is not uniformly faster: in the same BENCH.md STL Sort is 1105.64 ms vs M*LIB Sort 1706.60 ms (STL 1.54x faster; stable sort 1237.25 vs 1285.71 ms, close) and STL SSet(Rbtree) 2627.84 ms beats M*LIB SSet(Rbtree) 3092.66 ms (the win is the B+tree). Seq(Deque) 896.94 vs 1799.15 ms, Seq(List) 971.39 vs 1193.67 ms and String Concat 535.55 vs 607.03 ms are smaller wins. The unordered-set test row labelled 'STL USet Longest(dict oa)' is std::unordered_set<int> (label copied from M*LIB in bench-stl.cpp): M*LIB dict oa 778.50 ms and dict 932.71 ms vs STL 6189.18 ms (7.9x and 6.6x, derived from page data). Ratios are derived from page data, not stated by the project. The M*LIB README Performance section shows only PNG graphs against GNU C++ STL v10.2, so the table above is the checkable evidence. The mlib commit pinned in BENCH.md (4acdfe4, 2026-07-22) is the current master head.

notes: All claimed numbers and derived ratios check out against the result-branch BENCH.md, and the harness is symmetric (same rand_get key/value order, same 50% hit ratio, C_N_UMAP_U64 = 20,000,000). Kept at A on public code + Makefile flags + EPYC 7763 + GCC via ubuntu-latest cc; if the orchestrator requires a printed compiler version for A, this falls to C (version only in a sign-in-gated CI log). The record's attribution of 'GCC 16.1' to the benchmark was wrong and is corrected.

tier_reason: First-party CSV (benches/results/mem_random_s2_final.csv) from public harness code (benches/memory_random_bench.cpp) comparing mc::memcpy/memset/memmove with ::memcpy/::memset/::memmove; all 18 rows and every derived ratio match, but the CSV states neither compiler, flags nor CPU (those appear only in sibling result files for other benchmarks) and the glibc version is unstated, so C.

corrections.caveats: The README and docs publish no numbers; the 'must demonstrate superior performance' line is a design principle. Only the benches/results directory has data, and the only micron-versus-external-baseline rows found are memory primitives against glibc, not the allocator or STL containers named in the seed guess (allocator results are before/after against micron's own earlier revisions, and sort_bench_std.cpp, heap_bench_std.cpp and stack_bench_std.cpp have no recorded results). The claim is selective: the sibling file mem_detail_s2_final_a.csv (same author) shows libc faster overall for hot memcpy (micron wins 170 of 513 cells, geomean libc/micron cycles 0.96) and hot memmove (45 of 182, 0.89), faster on all 14 cold-cache memcpy cells (0.85) and on 11 of 14 cold memset cells, with libc far ahead at tiny sizes (for example memmove at 3 bytes 0.27 vs 1.12 cycles/byte); micron wins hot memset of zero (222 of 386, geomean 1.12) but not memset of 0x5A (21 of 50, 0.98); mem_detail_s2_final_b.csv gives the same picture. The random-size win applies to working sets of 32 KiB to 1 MiB only (all cache-resident on the 20 MiB L3) and is stable across the nine mem_random_*.csv runs (memcpy 1.36x to 1.64x at 256 KiB to 1 MiB), but the earliest mem_random_baseline.csv had libc faster at 32 KiB for all three ops. The harness subtracts a no-op batch, measures micron immediately before libc in each cell and does not check that the micron output equals the libc output. First-party, single machine (Haswell-E, an older CPU than glibc's newest ifunc tuning targets), glibc version unstated, compiler and CPU absent from the cited CSV, so tier C. Ratios are derived from page data. The abcmalloc component is MIT-licensed; the rest is BSL-1.0.

notes: Numbers verified exactly; the selective-win caveats (detail CSV counts and geomeans) were recomputed and match file a. No correctness bug found, but the harness never compares outputs, so a wrong-result fast path cannot be ruled out from the bench alone.
